segments.say: Lesson 6. Caching. Cache-aside, write-through, write-back, eviction (L R U/L F U), T T Ls, C D N, and cache stampede / invalidation.

A cache keeps a copy of frequently used data somewhere much faster (usually memory) so you don't redo slow work, like querying the database, every time. Here is an analogy. Keeping your most-used tools on your desk instead of walking to the storeroom each time. The storeroom (database) is the truth; the desk (cache) is a fast copy that can go stale.

Why does this matter? The single biggest performance lever in most designs. Brings tricky questions: staleness, invalidation, stampedes. A few key words. Cache hit / miss: Found in cache / had to go to the source. T T L: Time-to-live: auto-expire after N seconds. Eviction (L R U): When full, remove the least recently used item. Invalidation: Removing stale cache entries after data changes. Redis: The most popular in-memory cache.
Cache-aside (lazy loading). Request: G E T /product/42.
1. App checks the cache for key product:42.
2. Cache miss. It's not there yet.
3. Read from the database.
4. Store the result in the cache with a T T L, then return it.
Next request: cache hit in ~1 ms, no D B load. Read-heavy apps often hit 90%+ ratios.
On update: write the D B, then delete (invalidate) the cache key so the next read reloads fresh data.
L R U eviction. Cache is full: A is least recently used, D most recent.
Access B: it moves to the "most recent" end.
Insert E: no room, so evict the least recently used, which is A.
E is in. L R U is implemented with a hash map plus doubly linked list: O of 1 get and put. A classic D S A question too!

Write strategies. Cache-aside: the app manages the cache (read: check leads to miss leads to D B leads to set). The most common. The cache only holds what's read. Read-through: the cache library loads from the D B on a miss. Write-through: write to cache and D B synchronously. Fresh cache, slower writes. Write-back (write-behind): write to cache, flush to D B later. Fast writes, but data is lost if the cache dies. Write-around: write to D B only; the cache fills on read.

Hard problems. Invalidation: T T Ls plus delete-on-write. Accept bounded staleness. Cache stampede (thundering herd): a hot key expires and thousands of requests hit the D B. Fixes: request coalescing / locking, staggered (jittered) T T Ls, refresh-ahead. Hot keys: replicate them or add a local in-process cache. Cache penetration: repeated lookups for keys that don't exist. Cache the "null" result or use a Bloom filter.

Where caches live. Browser leads to C D N leads to A P I gateway leads to app in-memory leads to distributed cache (Redis / Memcached) leads to D B buffer pool. Cache as close to the user as correctness allows.

Say it in the interview. "For read-heavy data I'd use cache-aside on Redis with T T Ls and invalidate on write, L R U eviction, jittered T T Ls plus request coalescing to prevent stampedes, and a C D N for static and public content. I'd state the staleness the product can tolerate.".

Let's compare. Cache-aside: app checks cache, then D B, D B, then invalidate cache, simple, resilient, first read slow; brief staleness. Write-through: cache, cache plus D B together, cache always fresh, slower writes. Write-back: cache, cache now, D B later, very fast writes, data loss risk. Write-around: cache, then D B, D B only, no cache pollution, recent writes miss.

Redis versus Memcached. Data types: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams, strings only. Persistence: optional (R D B/A O F), none. Replication / cluster: yes, client-side sharding. Extras: pub/sub, Lua, T T L, rate limiting, leaderboards, simple, multithreaded.

A likely interview question: How do you keep a cache consistent with the D B? A strong answer: Cache-aside with delete-on-write plus T T Ls as a safety net. Accept bounded staleness, or use write-through where freshness matters. For strict cases use versioned keys or skip caching that data.
That's it for Caching. Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
